# forge v0.11.0-rc.1 — Forge has a key of its own

A release candidate, and the first one that changes how Forge gets onto a
server. It stops using your SSH setup — your keys, your agent, your
`known_hosts` — and starts using a key it made itself. **Upgrading needs one
manual step per server**, described at the bottom; without it Forge cannot reach
the machines it reached yesterday.

## Why

Forge has always connected as *you*, by borrowing whatever the machine it runs on
already had: the agent, or the first readable key in `~/.ssh`. That is a laptop's
answer to a question a phone cannot even hear — there is no agent there, no
`~/.ssh`, and no `ssh-keygen` that ever ran. It was never really an answer here
either: "the key I happen to have" is not something Forge can promise a server
anything about, and it meant the same repository got pushed under two identities
depending on whether you or Claude ran the command.

## `forge setup`

```sh
forge setup
```

Makes this device an Ed25519 key, keeps it in `~/.forge`, and prints the one
line that goes into a server's `authorized_keys`. Nothing else creates it — not a
first connection, not `host prepare` — because a key that appears as a side
effect is one nobody decided to trust. Run it again whenever you add a server: it
prints the same line and changes nothing.

## Forge's own SSH client is what runs now

The client built in v0.10.0 and shipped switched off is the default. Commands,
terminals and port tunnels all go through it, and it reads nothing of yours:
the device key, and `~/.forge/known_hosts`, which it writes itself on first
sight.

`FORGE_SSH_BACKEND=exec` puts the `ssh` binary back for one command — the way to
tell "is it the new client, or is it me". The CLI's own interactive sessions
(`forge workspace ssh`, `claude attach`, `expose`) still hand your terminal to
`ssh`, because they hand over the terminal you are sitting at; they are given the
device key with `-i`.

## A new workspace lets in this device

`forge workspace create` writes the device key into the workspace's
`authorized_keys` — not whichever public key the machine happened to have. It has
to be that way round: a workspace without it is one Forge could create and never
open again. `FORGE_PUBKEY` still works, and now adds a key *beside* it instead of
replacing it, so you can keep a way in from a plain terminal.

## Agent forwarding is gone

`-A` came off the workspace shell. Git on a server runs under the identity
`host prepare` put there, which is the one registered on GitHub; forwarding your
agent on top of it only obscured who was pushing. Revoking a device no longer
touches GitHub at all.

## Upgrading from v0.10.0

Your servers do not know this device's key yet, so the order matters.

**1. Install, without touching the servers yet:**

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marb-AI/forge/main/install.sh \
  | FORGE_VERSION=v0.11.0-rc.1 FORGE_SKIP_AGENT_UPDATE=1 sh
```

**2. Make the key and copy the line it prints:**

```sh
forge setup
```

**3. Put that line on each server — from your own terminal, with your own
`ssh`, one last time.** Both places: the login Forge connects as, and every
workspace that already exists (they were created with your old key and would
otherwise stop opening).

```sh
ssh <the target from `forge host list`>

KEY='ssh-ed25519 AAAA…'   # the line from step 2, quoted

mkdir -p ~/.ssh && touch ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
grep -qxF "$KEY" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys || printf '%s\n' "$KEY" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

for f in /home/workspaces/*/.ssh/authorized_keys; do
  grep -qxF "$KEY" "$f" || printf '%s\n' "$KEY" >> "$f"
done
```

(The loop needs to write into other users' files, so run it as root or under
`sudo sh -c`. A host with no workspaces yet will simply match nothing.)

**4. Back on your machine:**

```sh
forge host update      # the agent, now that Forge can get in
forge forwarding start # respawns the tunnels that failed to authenticate during the install
```

Then open the UI and check the things that use each login: a workspace shell and
a Claude session (workspace user), the host shell and the server metrics (admin
login), and a tunnelled port.

If something cannot connect and you need it working immediately,
`FORGE_SSH_BACKEND=exec forge …` goes back to the old behaviour for that one
command — and it being a release candidate, that is worth telling me about
rather than working around.
